title: The journal
hook: he kept a journal, mostly about the woods

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was life without principle: Thoreau's warning about a life spent only getting a living. Your line was more than a living.

"Do you keep a journal?" That, more or less, is what a friend asked Thoreau. Some readers take the friend to be Emerson; the entry doesn't name him. The journal's very first entry records the question and says, in effect: so I make my first entry today. No grand plan, no vow. A friend asked, and he started. That small beginning became a habit, and the habit became the place where much of his life as a writer actually happened.
screen: `DO YOU KEEP A JOURNAL?` → `SO HE STARTS, THAT DAY.` → `A SMALL BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: First, the start. Not a revelation in the woods; a friend's question, and a decision to begin the same day. Second, what fills it: weather, birds, the color of a leaf, the sound of ice, a neighbor met on the road. Thoughts about books and God and politics are there too, but again and again the pages return to the woods, fields and rivers near Concord. It's a record of noticing. Third, the quarry. Readers who compare the journal with his books find early versions of passages that later went into them. It wasn't a diary of feelings so much as a workshop. He walked, he looked, he wrote it down, and some of it became Walden. Fourth, the line a day. You don't need his hours or his talent to borrow the habit. The journal's gift is that it makes you look. If you know you'll write one line tonight about something you saw outside, you go through the day a little more awake, searching for it: a cloud, a crow, the smell after rain. The line might be clumsy. That doesn't matter; the looking already happened. Thoreau kept his going and going. Yours can be a single sentence in a notebook or a note on your phone, as long as it's true and about something you actually saw.
screen: `A FRIEND'S QUESTION.` · `A RECORD OF NOTICING.` · `THE WORKSHOP FOR THE BOOKS.` · then, large: `ONE LINE A DAY.`

segments.voice: Go back over the last day and look only for something from nature: light on a wall, a bird you half heard, the air when you stepped out. Let one come forward without judging whether it's good enough. Then, silently, say it in one plain sentence: not pretty, true.
The journal. The notebook Thoreau began because a friend asked, and filled, page after page, with the woods. Today's word.
Your line: one line a day. The looking matters more than the writing. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who borrow Thoreau's habit often keep a nature journal, a short daily note about weather, plants or birds they saw, which trains the eye as much as the hand.
